utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, good afternoon. Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour and good afternoon my learned friend from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. There seems to be a problem. I wasn't following the transcript because -- yeah. It seems there is something wrong. Please bear with us, Mr. Wubben. We need your cooperation a little bit. There is something wrong. In the meantime, Registrar, I will confirm this later on when the transcript is going. Although today most of the time will be taken by the Chamber itself in asking questions, I do not want a situation with the same -- with Mr. Jones and his client being unable to communicate because of a language problem, I would take it. So I am instructing the registrar to provide without delay or with the utmost celerity an interpreter that has never worked with the Office of the Prosecutor -- that has never worked with the Office of the Prosecutor -- to sit by the side of Mr. Jones and to act as a -- interpretation purpose or go-between between him and his client should your client want to send him notes or explain things to you, because otherwise we will have problems. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's very kind and considerate of Your Honour. If we had had more time I would have looked into something of that nature. We have a primitive form of communication with my Bosnian and my client's English, but that would be greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime we can proceed once this -- I see that the problem has been solved. I think we will have to go through this once more. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please. I know that you have called it already, but I would like you to call it again for the record because the transcript doesn't show that you did.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. And good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, I'm afraid I have to ask you the same question again. I want to make sure that you can follow the proceedings in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think then I don't need to repeat to you that I have tried -- we are trying to get the registrar to send us someone so that you can communicate with your lawyer better. Yes, again once more I have to look to my left and ask Mr. Wubben. Appearances for the Prosecution, please, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also good afternoon to my learned friend of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers and Joanne Richardson; also our case manager, Ms. Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is John Jones and I appear on behalf of Naser Oric. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know there is an urgent motion asking for an adjournment after the end of the testimony of this witness. I think we should address that at the end of the testimony of this witness. In the meantime we will proceed with the witness straightaway and not keep him waiting unless there are other preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very short. When I looked into the transcript I noticed that there might be a question by Trial Chamber, and please correct me if I'm wrong. To what extent there are beside the aerial photograph we showed also other aerial photographs of Srebrenica. And if that is a question, I can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Forget it, Mr. Wubben. We were just passing a comment because the only photo that -- when I asked you: Do you have one in a reduced size that we can show to the witness, it happened to show us everything except what we wanted to see. So it's not a problem. More or less we have an indication where the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just to support you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Well, I do appreciate your concern, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, is there a problem? No problem. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Mujkanovic, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today we'll do our best to finish with your testimony. That also depends on your cooperation. The shorter you keep your answers and -- the better it will be. So please try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Yes, we had almost finished the re-examination. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have some questions left for re-examination, Your Honour, and I would like to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please. That's why I called you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Wubben: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, good afternoon. At the end of the court session last Monday we were dealing with the issue of measures by Naser Oric to prevent the burning and looting of Serb properties. Let me refer to the transcript on Monday at the end of the session, and I will quote your answer to the question why Naser Oric wouldn't have intervened in trying to curtail the burning and destruction of Serb properties. And I will quote you in your answer: "He was in no position to discuss this with civilians, but the most important reason, the paramount reason, was that there was simply no way to secure the areas." In addition to this opinion, Dr. Mujkanovic, do you recall having held another opinion in the past as why Naser Oric did not intervene, why he did not curtail this burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not comfortable with the suggestion that this witness -- it's ever been accepted that Naser Oric did nothing to curtail the burning and looting. The questions asked, and I'm just reading the transcript, hence the delay of getting to my feet, but it was all a question of possibility of doing anything. And for my learned friend to suggest that there was a wilful suggestion of Naser Oric not to prevent something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As long as that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, please, he's not suggested that. He's asking whether in the past or on some previous occasion he gave some other explanation why Naser Oric did not intervene. He's not saying that he gave an explanation that he did not or chose not to intervene. It could be anything. So the question you need to answer, Dr. Mujkanovic, is the following: Do you recall having held another opinion in the past as why Naser Oric did not intervene, why he did not curtail in burning and looting? Did you ever give another explanation that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my own opinion, which I will now reiterate. Under the conditions that prevailed in Srebrenica at the time, it was impossible to lead a normal life or to carry out any of the usual procedures in relation to just about anything. There were no courts and no public prosecutors in Srebrenica at the time. There was a shortage of qualified people to do those jobs. They had left Srebrenica; it was as simple as that. I said once that any attempt by anyone at all including Naser Oric to prevent looting by civilians, to prevent civilians burning villages would have amounted to a loss of his own credibility in the area. He had no mechanism at hand to protect property nor was he in a position to create conditions for those people to have some sort of a normal life. He would have compromised the confidence that he enjoyed with the local population. And I'm sure that would have led to clashes in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct to take it as your testimony that he would not -- that he chose not to compromise the people and thus taking the opinion not to take steps or measures to prevent that burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about compromising the people. I'll say it again. It's very difficult to form conclusions on the basis of what actually happened in Srebrenica. Srebrenica only had partial civil authorities which had jurisdiction over civil and military matters, but it didn't have a public prosecutor. I'm not sure that there were more than 50 people in the entire area with university education. Most of them were engineers; there were seven medical doctors, physicians; and five or six people with a degree in economics. I'm not aware of the presence in the area of a single lawyer, though, who could have set up a court of law. There was no procedure in place to prosecute people or to take any measures against any individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. If you continue like this you're going to be here today, tomorrow, and even Friday. You're not answering Mr. Wubben's question. You did not answer it before and you're not answering it now. The question is very simply put: Is it your testimony that Naser Oric chose not to compromise -- not to compromise the people, not to compromise with the -- chose not to take steps or measures to prevent that the burning and the looting, so not to come and to clash with the people in the general opinion? This is basically what you are being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, again Mr. Wubben is putting words into the witness's mouth. What he was talking about was that for Naser Oric to be attempting to prevent an impossible situation he would lose credibility with the people; he didn't say Naser Oric chose to do anything. And if we're going to fairly summarise this witness's evidence, he also said that Naser Oric wasn't competent, either. He said it was the War Presidency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's an argument, that's a submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour -- No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones, it's a submission. Please sit down and let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want his evidence to be summarised fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been summarised more than fairly, Mr. -- and you will see later on how fairly it has been summarised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if I may, I would like to rephrase the question taking the words literally from -- exactly from the witness. What he meant by compromising the confidence of the people that the people had in Naser Oric, what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that he would have lost his credibility with the locals by doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- thank you. And in addition to that does that mean that he abide by the public will, that he followed the public will?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can answer that question, whether he was in compliance with the will of the people or the public. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean you don't recall that you ever gave such a reasoning or clarification?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I have ever said that, but it's certainly not something I can say whether Naser Oric followed the will of the people or the public. It's much too complex a question for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I refresh your memory that you in the past gave an opinion like that -- this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to be specific -- yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, this witness doesn't seem to be having any troubles with his memory. I don't see what the memory-refreshing exercise is supposed to be about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has to be specific. At this point you have to be specific. It's too generic. We could have discussed this with 101 purpose even with the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall you shared this opinion as a reasoning that -- as one of the reasons that Naser Oric followed the public will in the past with an investigator, giving a statement to an investigator, an investigator of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't follow the question even. What opinion? What reasoning? It's completely unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I clarified it, the specific reason of following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have to clarify it a little bit further. Did you ever discuss this with an investigator of the OTP? This is what you are being asked. And if you did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you did, do you recall what your position was? This is what you are being asked, basically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position and conviction at the time was as I have just stated. The phenomenon of arson and burning was rife in and around Srebrenica. I didn't hear Naser Oric say that people should burn things. It was simply something that was happening and there was no way to stop it. When asked why I believed it couldn't be stopped, I provided the same position as I have today. I also added is that one of the reasons may have been that he feared he would compromise the trust of the people and the fighters that he led.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dr. Mujkanovic, can I assist you in that respect that I will quote from your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, I have legal submissions regarding any reference to prior statements. I certainly didn't refer to them at all during cross-examination, so firstly this doesn't arise from cross-examination, but in fact I have lengthy submissions which I would like to make in the absence of the witness. I think it's become timely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it if there are submissions, on what, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, on a party seeking to impeach their own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- so far we haven't an indication that they -- that the Prosecution is trying to impeach their own witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, they're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're saying so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't see any memory-refreshing exercise which is justified. This witness hasn't been asked if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Jones. I can assure you that we are more than prepared, the three of us, in case there is even the slightest indication from the Prosecution that they are trying to discredit their own witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At that moment I have no submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you we are more than prepared. We have been prepared from the very first question. Yes, Mr. Wubben -- I suppose because you come -- I better make it clear, but I see that you are flanked by lawyers coming from common-law jurisdictions who are very familiar with the system. In the adversarial system, a party producing a witness is not allowed to discredit that witness. However, if that witness becomes an unfavourable witness or moves a step further and becomes an adverse or hostile witness, then the party producing that witness can be authorised to cross-examine the witness. This is the procedure that will be used -- in other words, you will not be allowed to try and discredit the witness before first getting our authorisation. Mr. Jones, will you explain to her why she's here so that we don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I mean, we'll give Mr. Jones a chance to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have a modus operandi already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the accused if he needs to communicate with you he will pass on papers or call you, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is an order in which you can proceed, but you can't just tell him -- lump it on him the way just you've been doing it. So go ahead, but do it in a proper procedure and manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And let me please confirm to you I'm aware of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so, but I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's why I used a phrasing of refreshing of the memory and my question "if he recalls so."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I would like to quote from your statement, Dr. Mujkanovic, my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. This is why -- do you recall having giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On one occasion only or on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would the witness please be showed the two statements that we are aware of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and I will just clear this up for the Prosecution myself. Am I right in suggesting to you that the first statement took place or was taken in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Over a period of three days, the 15th of January, the 16th of January, and the 17th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was longer. It was four or five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Usher, could you please show the witness the first of these statements. And, Witness, could you please have a look at that statement, the English version, and just confirm to me if you recognise your signature on any of those pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the person interviewing you? Were they Dan Perry and Eileen Gilleece?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember Dan Perry. I don't remember the other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown the second of the statements, the more recent of the two. Did you also give a statement to the Office of the Prosecution on or around about the 4th of June of last year, the year 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are being shown now the English version of that statement. Do you recognise your signature on any of the pages thereof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was the interviewing officer Mr. Nasir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now you may proceed, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me first address then and quote from your statement in 2000. In the English version that's page 18, Your Honour, and there are copies available of the statements I would like to tender. And page 18, the second paragraph, there is referring to the burning to the ground. And in the middle of it one, two, three, the fourth line there is a "mob mentality did occur," referring to that burning. Dr. Mujkanovic, do you -- can you read that part?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that particular section, page 18 you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the page in B/C/S would not correspond. Yes, page 18. Dr. Mujkanovic, page 18, the penultimate paragraph which starts with "Dozvolite da objasnim." And you are being referred to the part which starts "Istina je da je zavladao zakon rulje," et cetera. Read those four lines, please, and I don't know what Dr. Wubben [sic] wants to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did indeed a mob mentality occur and did Naser Oric followed that mob mentality?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been saying for six days now that the 80 to 100.000 people there were practically illiterate. They had the mentality of the mob. They were driven more by instinct than by reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your next question, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My next question will deal with the statement of 2004. That is ERN English version, Your Honour, 03577298.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just for the record state that in terms of memory-refreshing, the statement should really be contemporaneous with events, and this is 2004, some considerable time after events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that line may I refer to the fact that this is also a Defence exhibit number under D115, and that concerns the first two pages of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all I want to make sure that the witness has found the -- has the statement and he's got the B/C/S version. We're talking about of page 1 or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We're talking of page 2, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 2, all right. Did you find it, Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Starting with the words --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Halfway paragraph 4 of this statement --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and I quote you in part of that statement: "He," so Naser Oric, "followed the public will." And further on: "He chose the easy way out. He did not want to annoy the people and lose respect."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fairness to the witness, he also says Naser Oric was unable to stop that happening. I think the whole paragraph should be put to the witness, in fairness, rather than selectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is one paragraph which pretty much goes in favour of the accused, which we were going to highlight ourselves during our questioning. I suppose it doesn't vary at all from what he has told us earlier on in answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, it was in addition. He followed -- and those parts I quoted, Your Honour, as reasoning. He followed the public will. I didn't quote the part of being unable, because that's already his testimony. And also the part: He choose the easy way out. That's also a reasoning he did not so far answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what his previous testimony meant. If you reduce or distil the essence of it, that's what it amounts to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: With all respect, Your Honour, whenever he stated as a reason he chose the easy way out, that's another reason than being unable or following the public will or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he also says he was unable. In the same four lines, in one instance he says: "Naser Oric was unable to stop that happening," and then he also says that: "He chose the easy way out. He did not want to annoy the people and lose respect." We decide what to do with that and what significance to give it. But more or less it's exactly repetition of what he has told us already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So it might be possible for him to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you confirm? That's what we were going to ask him, Mr. Wubben. Reading this -- these last five lines of that paragraph in your paragraph -- I mean, it's five lines -- it reads as follows: "In fact it was kind of a public pressure to burn down the property left by the Serbs. Naser Oric was unable to stop that happening. He followed the public will. I think he should have been strict enough to stop the destruction of the property during the attacks; however, he chose the easy way out. He did not want to annoy the people and lose respect." Do you remember giving this statement to the officer, to Mr. Nasir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I do remember having said that. That's what I have been saying all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender these statements and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would object to tendering the statements. As far as the 2004 statement, as has been pointed out, that was a Defence exhibit for an entirely different purpose. I didn't raise the 2000 statement in cross-examination and for it to be tendered in re-examination when it wasn't something which arose from my cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not even the point. The whole point is: Why do you want to tender these statements, for what purpose? Because certainly they cannot substitute the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It can be used as evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not used to arguing with counsel, but I mean, this certainly calls for an explanation. What do you mean? In other words you mean to tell us that as far as you are concerned you can stop your re-examination of the witness here, tender his previous two statements, and submit that we also take into consideration at the end of the day as evidence the content of his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So what's the purpose of tendering these statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: As a clarification to the answers given to the Prosecution upon their questioning in these issues. Okay, Your Honour -- Your Honour, please enable me to confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you withdrawing your request, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I would like to withdraw my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Point taken. I think we have made ourselves clear. Have you finished with your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. I didn't know that. There is a long journey ahead now. So the witness needs to have the two statements in front of him --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I mentioned last week, that I would have submissions if Your Honours were to ask questions about the prior statement, I would be grateful for the opportunity to do that in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have a short break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He may even need to return to the hotel room. It's important points of principle which could take half an hour for me to expound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there's going to be a very short answer to them, Mr. Jones. You have to forget -- or remember that you're not in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I always know that, Your Honour, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you escort the witness to the room, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. As I say, there are a number of highly important points of principle which arise from Your Honours are to ask questions on the basis of prior statements. And since it doesn't just concern this witness but future witnesses, I want to set out in detail what our objections would be. And I can set them out in summary and then there are actually ten headings which might be helpful for Your Honours. But I would say in general, in my submission, there are very good reasons why you should not in this case the reasons which are set out which go to the heart of a notion of a fair trial and of the mainly adversarial proceedings of the Tribunal go into these prior statements. Now, if I can preface my remarks by saying this: The witness may have very good explanation for any apparent inconsistencies with prior statements; and to be perfectly honest, we too would like to hear perhaps what those reasons are. But that doesn't change the fact that for the reasons I've set out if the Prosecution and the Defence haven't gone into prior statements, then Your Honours shouldn't either, no matter how curious you are as to what has been said in prior statements. So now in summary, when prior statements haven't been put to the witness by either party - and I say this subject to the Prosecution's exercise of memory-refreshing today - but when during examination- in-chief and cross-examination the statements haven't been put and where the statements are in the exhibits, and I can deal with the 2000 statement as not being an exhibit, the 2004 is an exhibit for other reasons, we say it would be wrong for the Trial Chamber to put a single question on the basis of prior statements. Firstly, I would say it would amount to the witness being treated as hostile by the back door and moreover without the constraints and safeguards that would operate if the Prosecution made such an application; and that in essence you would be doing the Prosecution's job for them and being more royalist than the king if you were to do so. And even you might encourage the Prosecution not to make applications to treat witnesses as hostile but to rely on Your Honours to do the job for them. And in any adversarial system, and I'm aware I'm not in my system, but in a broadly adversarial for the Bench to treat a witness as hostile and cross-examine him on previous statements when the Prosecution hasn't made any application to do so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, let me interrupt you. You seem to preface everything on the wrong misconception that you have that, we want or we are trying to treat this witness as a hostile witness. He is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not everything is premised on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suggest that you make other submissions but not based on this. We are not even going to deal with this. I am making this clear. This is a misconception you have in your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course I have to anticipate that questions might be -- very vigorous questions might be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you might anticipate more before that that I as a Presiding Judge coming from a jurisdiction not much different than yours have more experience than you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Nonetheless, I have my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The second broad point, before I come to my ten subpoints, is that the understanding from the start of the trial is that Your Honours would have prior statements just to familiarise yourselves with the sort of evidence that the witness would be giving so that you would be better prepared to hear his testimony. So for the statements to then be used as a forensic tool, and they haven't been used by the parties, is a different use from one that was ever contemplated. And we indeed almost certainly would have opposed Your Honours having prior statements if we were to think that they might be used by Your Honours as a weapon entering into the gladiatorial contest, as it were, armed with prior statements to beat witness with; and as I say, it may be that that's not Your Honours's intention, but I need to set down the mark as far as that is concerned. Now, to go into the points in detail, and I'll take them briefly as I can. As I say, the prior statements haven't been referred to by the parties, subject to this afternoon which I'll deal with. In many cases where the parties agree to do so, prior statements are put to witnesses and they are made exhibits. And in this trial already that has happened in many cases that that's been done by either party. But the fact that it hasn't been done in this case is an important fact because Your Honour's questions, again as I understand it, are designed to clarify the testimony that has been given or the exhibits which have been submitted and where the witness hasn't gone into his prior statements and where the 2000 statement is not an exhibit, it's not a matter of clarifying testimony which has been given but embarking on a whole other exercise. My second point is, as I say, that the Prosecution has not applied to treat the witness as hostile. Now, that's a matter for them to decide and they may have reasons for why they make that decision. But the consequences of that decision, in my submission, should be accepted by Bench and the consequence is that the "prior statements" drop out as irrelevant. And the question of the hostility or adverse nature of witnesses is a very sensitive one hedged round by all sorts of procedural safeguards, and my concern -- and I'll cite a passage of impeachment of witnesses later. But there's a certain abuse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't want you to waste your time, Mr. Jones, but you're continually talking about hostile witness; adverse witness; impeachment of witness. There is no one trying to treat the hostile [sic] as adverse or hostile or trying to impeach the witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if the witness is even to be asked: If such and such wasn't true, why did you say that? then that's already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again you're taking it a step further. That's why I told you, please keep in your mind first and foremost that I have more experience than you do. Do you think I'm going to ask the witness why did you say so? Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I move to my third submission, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- which is: The paramount concern from all of us is that we get the best evidence from a witness. And another concern is that if the witness is pressed by the Bench, the authority of the Bench, not pressed but asked by the Bench about prior statements that he'll feel obliged to change his testimony and adopt the prior statement rather than to tell the truth. And that applies more broadly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, again, do you think that the Bench is going to ask the witness to change his testimony and adopt the prior statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, of course not, Your Honour. You wouldn't ask him to do such a thing. But if part of his testimony -- part of his prior statement is pointed out to him and the Bench is asking about it, he may be under the impression that he needs to adopt his prior statement due to the authority of questions of that nature coming from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He may feel that he owes us an explanation, but I don't think you can expect at any time from the Bench an invitation to the witness to change his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, precisely. It's that the witness will feel that he needs to adopt his prior testimony. And as I said, this concern applies more broadly -- Your Honours may or may not be aware that news agencies reporting on this proceedings in fact gave a lot of prominence to Your Honour's one question last week about a prior statement and on a very important matter about the presence or otherwise of Naser Oric at attacks. Now, other witnesses who may be coming to testify who will hear that will -- may be concerned that they're going to be given the third degree by the Bench, whether or not it's a true perception on their part, and again that they need to stick to the past to what they said in the past to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would expect that objection from the Prosecution, not from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If one has statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would help the Defence, not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not in all occasions, Your Honour. I'll come to the way in which statements are drawn up, which is another point I wish to come to. Fourthly, prior statements are not given on oath. What matters is surely what the witness says here in court. And in this respect statements to investigators differ in -- from two types of statements. In domestic proceedings you have statements that are given to a police with a perjury warning. For example in my system, Section 9 of the Criminal Justice Act of 1967 the witness is warned of the consequences of false testimony. We have an equivalent which is Rule 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. So we have "statements" which were given not on oath and only to ICTY investigators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, there is no chance, not even a fraction -- a fraction of a digit chance that his prior statements will replace the testimony that he has given here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My fifth submission is that the prior statement may well have been put together by asking leading questions, but spinning what was said into something more serious than was actually said. We have actually --even before that we have the problems of interpretation. But even here in court - and it's not meant as a major criticism of my learned friends - but they will ask leading questions on occasions, I can imagine how greater the risk of ICTY investigators spending days with the witness, asking a serious of leading questions, and then having a statement drawn up on that basis, which is very far from what the witness actually said. So again there is the danger if the parties haven't in an adversarial setting got into that issue for the Bench to pose questions on something which is so uncertain, which can be so uncertain. And we suspect that in this case that may be what's happened, given that the witness gave the same account that he's given here in the Telering programme, which we saw the transcript of, and in the interviews to Sheri Fink for the "War Hospital" book and it's the statements to the ICTY investigators which are the anomaly. We saw already one part of the 2000 statement which was self-contradictory in the sense of, talking about an inability to stop something from happening and then saying it was the easy way out. We have another example on page 15, sixth paragraph of the 2000 statement, where the witness appears to be saying that all radio users had to be authorised by Naser Oric and the radio operator was always present, and then in the next line: I used the radio without Naser's permission to contact my wife in Tuzla. A straightforward contradiction which an intelligent witness presumably never, never said. At another part, page 17 of that statement, the witness is stated as having said: "Each soldier would decide personally whether to take a prisoner or to shoot a prisoner. It was also the soldier's choice to decide what manner they chose to kill someone." Now that was such an absurd statement that in fact in the proofing notes which we received from the Prosecution the witness had corrected that. We have the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we don't have, the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That comes to my other point, Your Honour. For the exercise to be meaningful, if you don't have the proofing notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't have the proofing notes. In fact, I was going to ask for them straightaway if they exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will give you a copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because in the proofing notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very important, Mr. Jones. That's the only thing with sense -- I mean in inverted commas, valid, as a valid argument that you have submitted from the whole list because you have pre-empted what the exercise that we are going to embark upon, not knowing what we are going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, well hopefully I'll start making more sense for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, very simply put, are going to go through certain parts of these two statements and simply ask the witness whether he recalls having made that statement, full stop. And then if he wants to make any comments, he will make them. We will not invite him to make any comments unless he chooses to. But I would definitely -- If there was during the proofing there were proofing notes, that will make our exercise much easier. We want to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will provide them. We will make copies of them and provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was my seventh point which I was coming to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a very valid point, Mr. Jones. You don't need to labour it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My sixth point is -- concerns regarding the specific investigators involved in taking this statement and we're not prepared and we think the Bench should not be prepared to accept the bona fides of all persons employed by the OTP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not an issue. Again, that's why I'm repeating -- I'm telling you what the exercise is going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just we have evidence from Ms. Manas that Ms. Gilleece was actually negligent on one occasion of dealing with documents not being if'd and miff'd. I have the reference for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic has got a brain like you and I have, and if there is anything in that statement that he doesn't agree with, I suppose he can say, I'm sorry, Judge, that's not correct. I never said it. Full stop. And we won't ask him questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It may be for that point, Your Honour, it's nonetheless that we do need to submit to Your Honours at some point so you know what weight to give to statements which are given, but I agree that's perhaps not a matter for this witness. My seventh point is that you don't have proofing notes and we'll dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's important and we need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The eighth point is really a question of fairness to the witness. This witness has not just made two prior statements, he's made lots of statements. He's made statements in the Telering programme, to Sheri Fink for the "War Hospital" book. So for the exercise to be meaningful, we would have to ensure also that Your Honours have all his prior statements so that you're not negatively influenced against the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, his prior statements are not going to substitute for his viva voce testimony before this Trial Chamber. That's the rule we follow and we're not going to budge on that. What he may have stated in other instances could have been used by you parties during his testimony; it wasn't. And we are just going to confirm that he may have made such prior statements. Then of course, I mean just to be fair with both parties, particularly with the Defence, if after our questioning you think that you need to put some questions to the witness, then you're of course -- what we are going to do is just clarify some issues. Then of course if you're taken by surprise, we will remedy that. But that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I come to a ninth point which is I submit the most -- perhaps the most persuasive which is as I said at the outset is the understanding Your Honours would have prior statements just so you could familiarise yourself with the evidence. It was discussed at the pre-trial conference, and I can pass up copies of what is said on that occasion. I'm afraid it's three pages each and I couldn't staple them. But if I could start reading what Your Honour said on that occasion and it's the 28 September, 2004: "This brings me to an issue that I know was raised during the 65 ter meeting on which I will dwell very shortly. Each of these witnesses, with the exception of the experts, et cetera, would have given statements to the Prosecution in the course of the years that preceded this trial. Now, I come from a jurisdiction where we would hear the evidence of the witness and we would not have at our disposal any witness statement made prior to the trial. As I said, that makes sense, first of all, where it is the rule, as it is in my country. And it makes sense also where you have a procedure, a system in place which would ensure in any case that when the case comes to trial, the Presiding Judge, with or without a jury, would have at least the committal proceedings at his disposal."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Counsel kindly slow down for the benefit of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. "Over here, you get a list like this showing Miladin Sic [phoen] giving evidence. It's true, we also have very short, succinct summary of what supposedly this gentleman is supposed to testify upon. But we come here and basically we are the last -- the least persons to know what this gentleman is going to testify about. "This is a matter that has been discussed at length amongst us Judges," et cetera. And then I drop down. And then explaining the reason why Your Honours wish to have the witness statements: "First of all, certainly not because we want to influence ourselves negatively. We are three expert, experienced Judges, I mean, so we are not a jury. We are -- in other words, the reason why we require these to be made available is that we know beforehand what the witness is going to testify about, what he stated to the offices of the Prosecution," et cetera. So two points arise from that: Firstly, that is the reason it was an aid for Your Honours, not a forensic tool to be used in the proceedings. And if the use changes we feel that we have been misled, obviously not deliberately. But we are confronted with this situation which is not something which we agreed on and which we would have opposed at the outset if we knew the statements would be used as a forensic tool. And Your Honour expressly said there the purpose was not to influence yourselves negatively. But I fear that Your Honours' minds are influenced negatively against this witness and that you've stated that things he's said call for an explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: An implicit criticism that the witness has been inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you prefer to put it that way, I suggest to you that is the only wrong way you can put it. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would submit that the prejudice can only be avoided by the Trial Chamber if Your Honours banish the statement from your minds once it hasn't been raised in evidence by the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that really comes to my tenth point which as Your Honour said explicitly at the hearing of the 9th of December, 2004, page 2843, these proceedings are broadly adversarial; and of course it's an ongoing debate to what extent their inquisitorial features. If the prior statements are to be used by the Bench when the parties haven't entered into a discussion or haven't entered into putting to the witness parts of his statement, then they're been used in an inquisitorial way by the Bench and that's means a very different procedure from the one which is so far followed. So far, Your Honours, in these proceedings I've sought with various witnesses to have shown inconsistencies in prior statements, and to be perfectly honest, I've been given short shrift by the Bench on various occasions when I have done that. Fair enough. It's an adversarial proceeding; I'll take those points and the Prosecution will take those points. We've never asked Your Honours to intervene on our behalf to show that a Prosecution witness has made inconsistent statements and we wouldn't expect you to intervene on the Prosecution's behalf and to do their job for them of seeking to show prior inconsistencies. And Your Honours, that arose, Your Honour's statement that the proceedings were broadly adversarial, when as you may recall my colleague, Ms. Vidovic, was cross-examining Mr. Popovic about the provision of documents to Mr. Nikolic. And she opened the floor for Your Honours to ask questions because it seemed it might be an important issue of an attempt to interfere with the administration of justice. Your Honour said: We're happy with what he said; this is an adversarial system. Well, if it is adversarial, then fine. But that means that if neither party has dealt with prior statements in the way that Your Honours propose to, then Your Honours should not do so either. In fact -- I mean, if Your Honours only conduct that exercise when there has been apparently unfavourable evidence given in prior statements weighing in, to all appearances, on the side of the Prosecution, that would give rise to grave concerns about the appearance of a fair trial. Really, in fact in accordance with the principle in dubio pro re, you should come to our aid, although of course we don't ask you to, but the appearance of justice is terribly important. So in short, I would ask Your Honours to exercise judicial restraint in this instance. We all may be curious why things appear in the statement which were not said here, but I would ask Your Honours to overcome your curiosity and in a broadly adversarial system, accept that if the parties haven't dealt with it, Your Honours shouldn't either. Unless I can assist you further, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Do you have any submissions in regard, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Very short, Your Honour. Though it might have an answer of an adversarial system in Rule 89 (D) it is clearly confirmed that Judges can put in any stage of the trial any questions they like to, so with puts a kind of initiative role on the Bench whenever they want to clarify some issue. And I rely on the discretion from Your Honour. I said 89, it's 85 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 85 (B).

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 85 (B), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Further, when it comes to the differences within the adversarial system, it might be so that there is a very broad discussion possible between Defence counsel and myself as it comes to a pleading that though it might be adopted as such in the -- as a general rule, there is certain a discussion also among criminal-law system as well as in the Tribunal to give some weight at least to prior statements given by witnesses. And that's even confirmed as such in the Akashu [phoen] Appeal Chamber judgement of the 1 June 2001, where it is stated that a prior statement did indeed have some weight, albeit considerably less than in-court testimony. There is more to argue in that respect. But mainly I rely on the discretion of this Trial Chamber to rely on the -- Rule 85 to enable the Bench to put questions forward to the witness as to clarify an issue. And will you please bear me a moment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I just remind both of you that even in the purely adversarial system, although the Judges very rarely intervene, there is the inherent right to ask questions and, provided it's after the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, to ask questions which -- clarifying questions, provided that the parties then in that case are given the opportunity to put further questions should it be the case. But our system, although being broadly adversarial - of course I can confirm that - envisages a mixture of the two systems and definitely not only incorporates in the rules the specific right of the 85 (B) of the Judge at any stage to put questions to the witness, but most importantly of all - and this is where the concept of having these prior statements available for the Judge arises from in this instant - that we are called upon to give a reasoned decision. And there is no way we can reach a reasoned decision if we have not at our disposal at least the prior statements of witnesses. That is as almost a sine quo non. Having said that, it's definitely not the role of the Judges to take over the Prosecution's role or the Defence counsel's role; that's your role. As required by our procedure, we have given you all the time to have -- conduct your examination-in-chief, interrupted you very little; and we have given you, Mr. Jones, also all the opportunity to cross-examine the witness, interrupting you, again, very little and only if as and when necessary. You are also overlooking paragraph (F) of Rule 90 which is perhaps -- which perhaps crowns it all and which entrusts on the Tribunal the important role, primary role, of ascertaining the truth. There is no way we can ascertain the truth if we accept everything that you have submitted, Mr. Jones. We will of course exercise all the restraint that is called for in the circumstances, taking into consideration of course that the Prosecution did not try to impeach or discredit their own witness. Neither will we, because it's not our intention to try and discredit this witness. That could have been the way chosen by the Prosecution if they felt they ought to discredit him. But obviously we take it if they didn't -- they did not feel the need to discredit that witness, and that of course goes on the record. The same applies to your cross-examination. I mean it's -- you put all the questions that you needed to put. Obviously the information that the witness has given calls for some clarification. And what is -- what we are going to do is: We are going to make use of his previous statement, which are of great help to us in leading us and giving us an idea what kind of a clarification we can ask or we can seek from the witness. Of course I repeat: Whether the witness is a credible witness or not will ultimately be something that we are charged with deciding. But we cannot decide whether he is a credible witness or not and whether he is credible in whole or in part or whether he is not credible at all, if we are not given the opportunity to ask for some clarifications from him. So that's how we are going to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record I do want to reiterate, notwithstanding what Your Honour said, my absolute opposition to the course which Your Honour will pursue. I need to preserve that, obviously, for appeal. My point really is that there is no need for clarification in light of what he said; it's only in light of the prior statements, and they were never intended for that purpose. That's my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But thank God we have them, because otherwise we wouldn't have even realised that there were things that needed to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My second concern, if I could just place it on the record: The exercise is going to be selective and that you can't go through a 30-page statement. And if this witness is only asked about incriminating things he said against our client the appearance to the public may be an attempt to resurrect bad evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why, why, why, do you bring that issue -- raise that issue at all? Who said we're going to be selecting, and even -- You're becoming paranoiac. He said a lot of things against your client on matters that are not related to this indictment. Do you think we are going to ask the witness on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed, but on matters relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, Your Honours: I just would implore Your Honours to always ask questions that are fair to us and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will see for yourself that we will be asking the witness to confirm statements that he made to the Office of the Prosecution that go exclusively in your client's favour, which have not been mentioned either by you or by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then I stand to be corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but we will ask him other questions, too. So could we have the proofing notes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Here are the copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suggest that we take a short break to read them because if they clarify certain matters that we intended -- we can go through them now because I know exactly what questions we are going to put. We will have a short break. Can I ask the cooperation of everyone and have a 20-minute break instead of a 25-minute break -- I can't see behind the dark? Yes. The technicians?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll withdraw for 20 minutes and we'll resume soon after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just -- Usher, you could -- could you escort the witness in, please. In the meantime just for the record I know because I've already been given the information that it transpired during the break that in spite of my exhortations and instructions that the interpreter put at your disposal would be someone who has never worked for the Prosecution. I have been informed that there is no such interpreter in this Tribunal and that the lady who is sitting next to you has done some interpretation work with the Prosecution; however she is now with the registry and she is bound by secrecy, confidentiality. So for the record I wanted to know -- wanted to make sure that there is no substantial objection from your part. And I understand there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have no objection whatsoever. I trust entirely in the professionalism and ability of the interpreter and am very grateful to CLSS and OLAD for providing that at such notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and I also thank CLSS and appreciate -- because I understand that I was asking for the impossible. Yes, please escort the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, first of all my apologies to you for the interval that we had but before I undertake this exercise on behalf of the other two Judges and on my own behalf, there were some submission to be heard. We have heard those. Of course, the submissions did not concern you, so don't worry about what I have just said. I just want to express my regret that you had to wait in the room for some time. Yes, what's the problem? We have the same problem as before, so that means that I have to -- Can I proceed? I did not see the words scrolling. So there must be a problem. Dr. Mujkanovic, be patient with us. Bear with us. All right. So I don't think I need to repeat what I said. The witness has heard me. As I said, I will be putting the questions to you, questions that I prepared but also questions that the other two Judges prepared. We agreed I would put them all myself for practical purposes so that we get through this exercise as quickly as possible. One question that I meant to ask you I have already asked you and you have already given the answer. You made two statements: One in 2000 and one in 2004 and you have seen both statements. I want to make sure that you still have them in front of you.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first starts with the following declaration: "I give this statement of my own free will and voluntarily. I have not been made any promises nor have I been forced to make this statement by any person or entity." Are these your words or are these the words of the person who was drawing up the statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person drawing up the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were you sent for or did you just appear and volunteer a statement? Were you sent for by the Office of the Prosecutor or did you just go to find an officer of the Prosecution and told him or her I want to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain how it was. It was back in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a phone call from a person who said he wanted to meet me. I asked what it was about and he said there was a humanitarian organisation that wanted to speak to me. I asked: What humanitarian organisation? And he said, they're from The Hague. We wouldn't like to explain anything else. The first time they came there were two men and one woman. They spoke to me for half an hour informally and they said they would come to see me again. That was in late 1999. They returned. We spoke for a longer time, perhaps for two hours, and they said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Because again, I want to get through this exercise as quickly as possible. In other words, it's not you who looked for the Office of the Prosecutor; it's the Office of the Prosecutor that looked for you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. They looked for me on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number one. And do you confirm what is stated here, that you were not made any promises? And that --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now please go to - this is going to be a problem now - page 10 of your 2000 statement. You mention there Major Rizvanovic's 16th Muslim Brigade. Later on you tell us that it was established in Zagreb. Where was it based? It was established in Zagreb, as you tell us; but where was it based?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tuzla. And my other question in relation to this: It says: 16th Muslim Brigade. Does it mean that there were at least 15 other Muslim brigades or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means nothing. It means nothing. It's just what someone decided to call it, probably the person who established it. It was set up in Zagreb by refugees who ended up in Zagreb, refugees from the Podrinje area. They were given uniforms and transferred to the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to answer my question. These are very simple questions that I am going to put to you and they only require or call for a very simple answer. My question was: I see here "16th Muslim Brigade." That calls for some clarification. Does that mean that there were at least 15 other brigades? And if there was a 16th, was there a 17th and 18th that you know of?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And that leads me to my next question that I was going to ask you, but again I will not ask you because this is the 114th now Eastern Bosnia Brigade. So could you please go to page 12.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And page -- sorry, not -- yes, page 12, last paragraph, which starts "Oko 4.00 sata 5 augusta 1992." You say: "On 5th of August, 1992, around 4.00 p.m. we reached Susnjari. Naser Oric was told over the Motorola radio that I arrived with my group. Oric radioed back that I should wait for him." How do you know this? First of all, did you make this statement to the officer interrogating you? Do you recall making this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically recall saying this. I know that I was told to wait for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you don't recall, you don't recall. Next question. You say -- you continue reading: "Naser Oric arrived in a small truck with 15 to 20 soldiers and Zulfo Tursunovic was also with him." Do you confirm having said so to the Office of the Prosecution? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "We drove off in a small truck. I was in the cabin of the truck with Oric, Tursunovic, and the driver was Mevludin Salkic." Do you remember giving this information of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you say: "At about seven we reached Srebrenica. We went to Naser Oric's command post. The command post was located at the PTT building which was the post office." Do you remember giving this information to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically remember the wording, but that was what happened. We were driven to the post office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could you now please go to the next page, page 13, and the paragraph starts with [B/C/S spoken]. The fourth paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 13, fourth paragraph from the bottom [B/C/S spoken]. Are you on page 13? Can --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's all right. I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to read it and then you just confirm to me the following. "I will tell you about our military. April 1993 was the time of demilitarisation." Do you remember saying this to the officer of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you continue: "Naser Oric's command compromised 12.000 men." Did you ever say this to the officer of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said that. That was the usual number mentioned, about 12.000 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you continue: "At that time everyone was a soldier." My question -- first of all, do you confirm having said so to the person interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to confirm that at this point. I can't specifically remember, and therefore I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Let's move to the next: "For example, it included the War Presidency, my staff, and those who were really fighting. The actual number of soldiers in the fighting was approximately 10.000 soldiers." Do you remember having stated this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you probably did, is there a reason why in 2000 you had no problem with using the word "soldiers," but you did have a problem using the word "soldiers" here? There were fighters; there were no soldiers, but fighters? Would you correct, in other words, what is written here? It's a clarification, not a contradiction; let me make it very clear to you. Because you explained to us what you meant during your testimony. But I want to make sure that you still mean the same.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used the term "soldier," and this was not a term used in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We spoke about fighters, not about soldiers. It may be a matter of interpretation, but certainly "soldier" was not a term that was used ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you for that explanation and clarification, Dr. Mujkanovic, and I move to the next. You need to go to page 14 in your text, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the first paragraph [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last sentence of that paragraph, you say with regard to the wounded prisoners that came to your hospital: "I did not see any signs of torture or abuse on any of the prisoners that were taken to the hospital and I treated each one of them." Do you confirm having stated this to the officer of the -- officer from the Office of the Prosecution interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next paragraph. [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "I had a condition that no one wears a weapon in the hospital."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember saying this to the -- stating this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably stated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then according to this statement it goes on as follows: "Sometimes Naser Oric would come into the hospital with his weapon on. I spoke to him about being a role model, but he always carried a gun; it's simply how Naser functions." Do you remember stating this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you add: "To my knowledge Naser Oric never went to the rooms to see the patients that were prisoners." Do you remember having made this statement to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Oric ever give you a reason for this or did you ever discuss it with Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I now ask you to go, please, to the same page, the penultimate paragraph, the one that starts with [B/C/S spoken] --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And go to the last part which --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where it starts [B/C/S spoken]. Okay.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And according to the person who drew up this statement, you said the following: "He then said: Here is the head of a Chetnik." Do you remember telling the officer interviewing you this or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I will be asking you this kind of questions to confirm whether you have told the Prosecution. If you feel at any moment that you need to clarify matters or that this is not exactly how you put things to the person interviewing you at the time, please draw our attention immediately and I will authorise you to say what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you condition: "He took the head and paraded it around the town." Do you remember telling this -- saying this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then you continue: "I know Naser Oric was on that offensive," in other words the offensive of the 8th of August. Do you remember saying this to the officer of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I didn't know at the time whether he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
