utterances.text: And then you say: "I do not know if Naser Oric saw the head." Do you remember stating this to the officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to clarify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this statement here, I was talking to Mr. Perry for four or five days about many different things. He probably took only what he needed from my account. His question may have been: Did Naser Oric see that head? I can hardly be expected to remember the questions he asked five years ago. If you take it out of the context, then that's what I appear to be saying. And my answer is: I don't know if Naser Oric saw the head. Much like I'm answering your questions now, he asked me all kinds of questions. And this went on for days. If my statement was complete, it would probably run into hundreds of pages. Here we see things taken out of their natural context. Therefore, it's very difficult for me to say now whether my specific wording was like this or not. I know there were many questions, many allegations, being made and I was being asked what my position was on a number of different matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said according to this statement: "The head had dark-coloured hair, but it is hard to say if it was black or brown since it was dark and the head was bloody." Do you remember saying this to the officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I saw and that's what I've said here, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next paragraph where you mention Kemo. I'm only interested in the last sentence of that paragraph which you find in the next page on page 15.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And according to this statement you told the officer: "Kemo was one of the men in Naser Oric's circle." Do you remember telling this -- saying this to the officer interrogating you or interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have put it that way, Your Honour, because Kemo didn't belong to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next paragraph. Can you follow me it starts with "Nakon ofanzive koja he izvrsena," top of page 15.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It reads as following: "After the offensive that occurred on the 8th of August, 1992, a few days later, maybe the 11th of August, Naser Oric, Akif Ustic, Zulfo Tursunovic, Hamdija Fejzic, some of Naser's men and I had a meeting at the PTT building." Do you remember saying this to the officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember having said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It goes on: "I told them I need to be allowed to prepare for any future offensives." Do you remember saying this to the officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that this is an issue that I discussed, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next paragraph: "Naser Oric and Akif Ustic are the men who made the decisions." Do you remember saying this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what words would you have said -- anything that you would like to tell us?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that this has been taken out of context. I also spoke about what I have testified about here. Naser Oric was the commander of the defence of Srebrenica and Akif Ustic was a sort of deputy of his. That's how he would call himself. He said he was the deputy of the command of Srebrenica. As to the question of who took decisions about such matters, I suppose that that was the sort of answer I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then it continues: "Hamdija Fejzic did not make decisions although he was the President of the Executive Council in the War Presidency in Srebrenica." Do you remember saying this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the question was about Hamdija Fejzic, about the role that he played. I said he was the President of the War Presidency of the Executive Committee in Srebrenica. And when asked if he took decisions of any kind, I replied that he didn't take any decisions, that he couldn't take any decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Next paragraph. It starts with this sentence: "I attended meetings with these men often." Do you remember having said this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this manner, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which manner would that be then?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that since the hospital was opposite the post office I would often go to the post office when I had breaks and meet certain individuals there and speak to them. But I didn't attend official meetings of any kind there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Further down in the same paragraph you have this -- these three sentences or four sentences which are joined, so I will read the entire four lines. "My personal role was to after the first offensive work on convincing the people in power to establish a properly functioning military organisation. The operational headquarters had to be established to know what everyone should be doing and who was responsible for what." Do you remember having said this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember having spoken about this, and in fact this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it continues: "Naser didn't like that. He perceived me as competition." Do you remember saying this to the officer of the Prosecution -- of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't remember that because I never spoke to Naser about that. Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next paragraph reads as follows: "I told Naser Oric that we should ask the professional soldiers under his command to help us run the affairs of the military in Srebrenica. I knew that there were four army officers that had finished the military academy and that there was four reserve officers from the former JNA. Naser would not allow these people to be part of the organisation, stating that they had to prove themselves in the field. We argued over this point, but I could not change his mind." Did you ever make this statement to the officer interviewing you? Do you recall making this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, I never spoke to Naser Oric about the formation of the operations staff. I spoke to this -- I spoke about this to Hamdija Fejzic and to others about forming the operations staff, and they told me that there were four officers who had just graduated. They were in Srebrenica, and they were reserve officers of some kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, same page, page 15, the paragraph before the last. [B/C/S spoken] 15 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "On the 15th of September, 1992, we had our first meeting at operational headquarters. The first offensive planned by the operations headquarters was the Podravanje area." Do you remember having stated this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this way. I said when the operations headquarters were formed, its role was to prepare for actions. And depending on the various fields that people were responsible for, each individual had to play the role assigned to him and perform his duties within that field. I wasn't even aware of the fact that an action of some sort was being planned. And I certainly could not have made such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you skip a paragraph and go to page 16.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It starts with "Prisustvovao sam sastancima." Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes three just follows. I'm only interested in the first sentence of that paragraph: "I would attend the meetings and listen to the discussions of how to organise the offensive. Naser Oric was the overall commander and all major offensive actions had to have his authorisation." Do you remember having said this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, firstly because as I have already said at most of those meetings I wasn't present, I didn't attend them, for the simple reason that I had a lot of work in the hospital. And in such cases, someone else would replace me. Here was Dr. Avdo Hasanovic. In this case it was Dr. Avdo Hasanovic. So as far as those meetings are concerned, I don't think what is stated here is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then again skip at the next paragraph and go to the one which starts with "Radio stanisu nije mogao svako koristiti." "Not just anyone could use this radio station. All users had to be authorised by Naser Oric and the radio operator was always present." Do you remember having ever stated this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in response to a question as to who authorised the use of the radio stations. That's what I was told when I wanted to use a radio station. I was told that Naser had to authorise the use of radio stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then continues: "I used the radio without Naser's permission to contact my wife in Tuzla. My wife was able to contact me on two occasions." Did you ever say this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably did because that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next paragraph, roughly four lines down: "I was never present when Naser contacted Sefer Halilovic, but Naser would tell me that he has reported to Sefer about his offensives." Do you remember saying this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's probably what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the last paragraph on that page, "Kao sto sam rekao." Right.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "As I said, we had meetings before the offensives. The purpose of the offensives was not solely to gain territory. Instead, many times the offensives were planned to get supplies, food, equipment, material, and things from the village attacked. Many times we chose villages that were rich in resources." Do you remember saying this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this way. I don't think the first person was used when he asked me where the offensives were prepared -- or rather actions not offensives, I probably said that there were offensives. But I wasn't present at those meetings so I couldn't have used the first person when relating this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next paragraph. The third sentence: "I had binoculars and I saw our soldiers burning the haystacks and other things being set afire by them." Do you remember having said this to the interrogator interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as it has been translated here. I've already explained this. I certainly wouldn't have said that there were soldiers. This is a term I never used. I never used the term "soldier." Secondly, as I have said, those two men weren't armed. So I couldn't have said that they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "Naser Oric had requested that they pick up hay, bricks, and other such items after an area was liberated and secured for the enclave." Do you remember stating this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have put it in this way; that's certain. I certainly didn't mention Naser Oric's name. I certainly didn't say that he requested that hay and bricks be gathered. I've mentioned how this was done in the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go to the last paragraph on page 17, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to this statement you told the officer, the interviewing officer: "We did not have a special unit in place to take care of the prisoners for the offensives. The main interest of soldiers was to get into an area, collect as much food and war booty as possible. It was thought that there is no gain in capturing soldiers." Do you remember telling -- stating this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's more or less what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Skip the next paragraph, please, and --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "After a village was liberated and we gained -- and regained the resources, there was no interest to maintain the village. During the liberation, three waves would occur. I myself did not understand why we did not keep the villages and move the refugees. Here is what usually happened." So far, would you agree that this is what you stated to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's more or less what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice sometimes that the witness isn't totally comfortable. Perhaps he could -- it could be clear to him, if he needs to add anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have made it very clear to him. Our questions, as I said, are very simple and straightforward requiring a yes or no with the caveat that I put in the beginning that if he feels he needs to tell us anything else he is free. We are not going to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless it's something that is very obvious. Otherwise he's free to tell us what he likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If there's anything he's unhappy with, he should tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the purpose of this exercise, actually. According to this statement it continues as follows: "Here is what usually happened. After liberation the first wave would be soldiers looking for ammunition and military resources. The second wave would be mainly civilian people and some soldiers. These soldiers were the ones who did not have weapons. They would search for war booty. They would look for weapons, ammunition, anything. Things like flour. Everyone was seeking something to allow them to trade. Rifles were needed. So if a soldier, who did not have a rifle but had a sack of flour, he could then trade the flour for a rifle if someone else found an additional rifle. That was what was occurring." Do you remember saying this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said and that's something I said here before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again I draw your attention to part of that statement, the second wave. "The second wave would be mainly civilian people and some soldiers. The soldiers were the ones who did not have weapons." Is this a correct reflection of what you said? Did you use the word "soldiers" on this occasion or did you use the word "fighters"?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I certainly didn't use the term "soldier." As you can see for yourself - perhaps it's a translation issue, it was translated twice - but these people were people who were looking for a rifle, for ammunition. I said that in that entire enclave anyone who had a rifle had to go to the front line to defend its territory, so rifles were just as important as food. I couldn't say that they were combatants if these people didn't have a rifle of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next paragraph: "The civilians, the women and children, would go through the houses and take everything else from all the houses and structures. The third wave would be some sort of groups, again civilians, who were good at finding things that were well-hidden. This group would poke sticks in the ground to search for buried ammunition, food, money, and cigarettes. And then after that, the burning would start. So no one wanted to live there." Do you recall having made this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could English interpreter speak into mike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next paragraph: "Sometimes civilians would get to the villages before the soldiers. They would be waiting in the area for the soldiers to attack. We were unable to control the civilians and it was not possible to keep our attacks secret from them. Hajrudin Avdic from the War Presidency suggested during meetings and at other times that something should be done about the people. Naser Oric recognised that the civilians were in the way of the soldiers. Naser told the soldiers to tell their relatives to wait until after the soldiers had liberated the village. Naser repeated that message many times to the soldiers. At meetings as well he told everyone to spread the word to civilians." Do you remember having made this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's more or less what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we go to the next paragraph now: "I never heard him," it means Naser Oric, I take it, "instruct his soldiers to tell the villagers not to burn the villages down." Do you remember having ever made this statement to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never made such a statement, Your Honour. It's been awkwardly translated. I never heard [Realtime transcript read in error: "heard"] Naser Oric ordering soldiers to set villages on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It continues. "Naser Oric's theory was that the houses should be burned down --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a problem with the transcript. I think he said I never heard Naser Oric ordering soldiers to set villages on fire." We've got the complete opposite in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't concentrating on the transcript. Please help me because I can't do two things at the same time. Yes, he did. I heard what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's line 16, page 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he said the opposite. Please confirm, Dr. Mujkanovic, that what you said was that you never heard Naser Oric ordering soldiers to set villages on fire, that you never heard, not that you heard.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard Naser Oric ordering combatants to set villages on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next question. "Naser Oric's theory was that the houses should be burnt down. He and I argued over this many times. Naser Oric said that if the houses are not burnt to the ground, we have not done our job because the Serbs will return. Naser Oric discussed this at meetings. At one of the meetings, I spoke up and asked them not to burn the buildings. I told him that it was not good for us to burn the houses. I told him to take whatever we need, yes, but not burn them to the ground." Do you remember having stated this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is partially correct. We did discuss the matter and I have frequently said here that setting fire to villages was one of the major problems in Srebrenica. We discussed the matter and tried to determine how to resolve this problem, but I never said that Naser Oric said that those houses should be burnt to prevent the Serbs from returning to them. I said that there was a rumour in Srebrenica, according to which these houses should be burnt to prevent the Serbs from returning to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next paragraph. It continues as follows: "Let me explain. In the enclave one man was at the top. Many people hopeless. Naser Oric was the top authority; he was like a king to the people. If Naser's theory was to burn the buildings to the ground, then both soldiers and civilians did that, and that was his theory. Of course not everyone participated." Do you remember having stated this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to add anything or should we take that as your complete answer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should -- would you like to add anything or would you like to leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't leave it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- yes, what would you like to state, if at all? I mean, you're not being forced to...

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that when this statement was taken we spoke about all sorts of subjects, and if someone took certain parts of my statement out of context and record them in this statement then this is the result. When we spoke about Naser Oric, I said that he was the commander of the defence of Srebrenica. As such he was the most respected person in the area. But the other people who were living in that territory were people who had lost all hope. It's true that we spoke about this and among other things I also spoke to Naser Oric about the necessity of finding some sort of solution about preventing those villages from being set on fire so that people could live there, et cetera. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, sorry to interrupt. I'm just wondering if we could receive some assistance from the booth. I'm having a little trouble hearing the English. The witness has a loud clear voice. The transcript-taker is having trouble too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had the same problem a while ago, so I increased the volume. I could barely hear the interpreter, the male voice that I was receiving at the time. Unfortunately the end result is that I am hearing myself too loud. That's the problem I have. I don't know. If this is a technical matter that can be attended to. MR. DI FAZIO: If he can speak up a bit from the interpreter's booth because we can hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter will try to speak more loudly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the problem. Sorry, Dr. Mujkanovic, I think we interrupted you. Have you finished or would you like to add anything else?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished. There's nothing else I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And then you continue: "A mob mentality did occur," something that you were referred to this morning -- sorry this afternoon, earlier on, "the psychology of the masses. There were people who opposed Naser Oric's ways, for example, Hakija Meholjic. There was almost an armed conflict between their troops. Fortunately that conflict was avoided." Do you remember having stated this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in these words. I did say that there was a permanent state of conflict between Meholjic and Naser Oric. I've said so during my testimony. I tried to bring them together several times, have them talk to one other to resolve the problems, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So now we go to page 19, please, the third paragraph from the top: Naser Oric [B/C/S spoken]. "Naser Oric had two press officers. They usually went into the villages after they were liberated and took photographs and videos of the result." Do you remember having stated this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be a mistranslation. Those were no officers. Those were just two people with a camera who recorded everything that went on in Srebrenica. They were no officers at all. I don't think this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then next paragraph: "Naser Oric, Oric had a lot of things to trade. The 50 men around Oric were like his personal unit. Sometimes they were referred to as his bodyguards. I know that each of those men had to bring whatever they acquired in the offensives to Naser Oric's special storage places. Naser Oric divided it up later." Do you remember having stated this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not like this. Not like this, Mr. President. As I said in my testimony, there was a storage facility at Naser's house which he used to store food for the fighters. But there was no trade in Srebrenica. That's certainly not true. And as for these 50 men who were with him, some sort of a personal unit, that is not true either. As I said, there was some people who were very close to Naser Oric, people he considered to be particularly brave fighters. Those people were usually in his vicinity, and I've given you the names of some of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Next paragraph: "Naser Oric had -- has storage places all over. One was in his house in Potocari. And the entire town of Srebrenica storage houses were under his control." Do you remember having stated this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not like this. I said what I said. I said there were two storage facilities under the control of the War Presidency, and there was one storage inside Naser Oric's house as I've explained. I've explained its purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Was Safet Omerovic still alive?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now it's the third paragraph before the last on page 19: "Naser Oric je posvuda imao takva skladista." "Naser Oric was the person in charge of maintaining a professionally organised military operation." Do you remember having made this statement to the officer of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably something that was taken out of context, the overall context of my interview. But as I have said, Naser Oric was Srebrenica's commander. So this is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll skip the second sentence of that paragraph. I take you down a few lines, you mention all the offensives that were dealt with during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is that sentence that I asked you about earlier on. I just want a re-confirmation from you whether you ever said it as it is, as it appears in this statement to the officer interviewing you. "Naser was physically at each and every one of these offensives, directing them." That is, Podravanje, Fakovici, Kamenica, Kravica, Voljavica, Bjelovac, Kunjarac, Loznicka Rijeka, Sase, Kravica area, Skelani, and Jezero." Did you ever state to the interviewing officer that Naser was at each and every one of these offences directing them?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sure I never said that, that he was physically present or led the offensives. This was not something that I was in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Page 20, there's a very short -- the third or fourth paragraph which starts with "dana 5. oktobra 1992. Pokrenuta je ofanziva na Fakovice." Right. Did you find it? Page 20 -- page 19 -- page 20, sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first sentence of that paragraph reads as follows: "On the 5th of October, 1992, Fakovici offensive was launched. The attack was organised by Zulfo Tursunovic and Naser." Do you remember having made this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, skip the next paragraph and we get to the paragraph which starts with: "Dana 6 ili 7 novembra 1992. Naser Oric je izvrsio napad na Kamenicu."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first sentence reads as follows: "On the 6th or 7th of November, 1992, Naser Oric launched an attack on Kamenica." Do you remember having made this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next paragraph which starts with: Dana 14 decembra 1992. Pocela je ofanziva za preuzimanje kontrole u muslimanskim..."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "On the 14th of December, 1992, an offensive to gain control of the Muslim villages Voljavica, Bjelovac, Kunjarac, Loznicka Rijeka and Sase was launched. Naser Oric commanded this offensive also." Do you remember making this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did state this but, again, this is out of context. There were other questions being asked, and when I was asked about the offensives and who led them I never said even at the time it was Naser Oric. But it is recorded the way we see it now. I do have to accept it, though --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I hope it's clear to the witness, he does not have to accept what is in his statement. He seems to be under the impression that he has to accept what is in his previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, you don't have to accept anything that is there. The purpose of this exercise is precisely to get clarifications from you.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't agree with what is written in this statement, please tell us so. That's why we are asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've said so right here. I'm under oath. I stand by all of my statements. Again, I must say that I had no personal knowledge then or now of Naser's involvement with any battle or action that occurred. Everything that is written here is something that I only saw several days ago in the Bosnian language. It was then that I said I had serious objections to the translation and to the contents of the statement, but then it was explained to me that this was a different jurisdiction, unlike the one that I come from. Through our preparation, Mr. Wubben and I clarified a number of things. I pointed out several translation inconsistencies and errors, which were subsequently corrected. We can take -- we can take it one step at a time and go through the whole statement, but I don't think this entirely reflects my original statement. These are bits and pieces taken out of context and included in this statement. If you look at this, what transpires is that I talked about Naser Oric, only it's just not true. I spoke about everything that was going on in Srebrenica at the time, much like the account I have given here to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it continues a couple of sentences further down: "The frontal attack would not have worked since the Serbs had fortified their positions in the villages. So Naser Oric, Zulfo Tursunovic, and other members of the headquarters decided to send diversion groups into the area." Do you remember having said so to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we spoke about that and this is more or less what happened, as I have confirmed to the Chamber when asked. I re-confirm it now. This is more or less how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if I invited you to read for yourself, in other words not aloud, this entire paragraph starting: "On the 14th of December, 1992," and ending with: "Mis is a very good friend of mine and we spoke often," what is not correct in that paragraph? What is not your words? What is in this paragraph that you never stated to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the paragraph. I never mentioned any names in terms of who commanded what. Whatever is stated here is something that I had been told by Safet Omerovic, nicknamed Mis. I never spoke about who exercised command over anything. Therefore ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the only part which is not correct, is not true, in other words you never mentioned it to the officer, is the part that reads: "Naser Oric commanded this offensive also"?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've said a number of times that I was not aware of the actions. I was not physically present at any of the actions, nor did I know that Naser Oric exercised command in any of those actions or what his role was in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's my question. I just wanted a confirmation from you that according to you you never said to so to the interviewing officer. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record that the witness's answer about not knowing about commanders would also cover the sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am coming to that. I am coming to that. But that part he did not deny, so I'm taking it that he is referring only to Naser Oric. You also mentioned according to this statement Zulfo Tursunovic. Did you mention Zulfo Tursunovic in relation to this offensive, particular offensive of the 14th of December, 1992? Or has the name of Zulfo Tursunovic been included here notwithstanding that you never mentioned it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have mentioned Zulfo Tursunovic but I was never in the position to say who exercised command or how. I could not have referred to Zulfo Tursunovic as a commander or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Skip the next paragraph, please, and concentrate on the following two paragraphs. And I refer you to the last sentence in each. The first paragraph: "In some instances, the civilians went into areas before our soldiers." That's the last sentence of the first paragraph. The last Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sentence of the second paragraph reads as follows: "The civilians were going into the area to retrieve the food because they were starving." Did you -- do you confirm having made these statements to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find this paragraph. Some Muslim civilians were killed during the air strike. Civilians were entering the area in order to get food because they were starving. Is that the one you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's the last sentence of the paragraph you have been reading. I've also referred you to the last sentence of the previous paragraph. The last sentence reads: "In some instances the civilians went into areas before our soldiers."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes civilians would enter certain areas before the soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You agree that you did make these two statements to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably so. But this is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you made this statement. Now page 22. Go to page 23, please, the third paragraph from the top. "Vise ljudi koje sam sreo u bolnici."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "I was told" -- I'm reading from the English page 22, fourth paragraph. "I was told by the various people that I encountered in the hospital that during the Kravica area offensive there was a lot of abuse which occurred in the village. The abuses happened when all the civilians swarmed into the area after the attack." Do you remember having made this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, taken out of context of the overall event. I don't agree that this faithfully reflects what I said. This was something I heard at the time. When civilians entered villages, there were acts of abuse being committed. Now, whether it's true or not is not something I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely not, you are not being asked to tell us whether it happened or not; that will be our task, difficult task, later on in due course. This is why we need your help. I mean, obviously if you were not there you cannot confirm anything. What I asked you was whether to confirm whether you made this statement, whether these three lines reflect faithfully what you told the interviewing officer. If they don't, please tell us so.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not faithfully, not as I said during the interview. It's just taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the investigator at the time that I was not physically present and that it wasn't something I could talk about. And then he asked me about hearsay, things that people talked about in Srebrenica at the time. It was that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The next paragraph, the first sentence only: "Both soldiers and civilians told me that our soldiers came into the village of Kravica that particular morning, which was Serb Christmas, and they killed all the Serbs in the village, including men, women, and children." Did you ever say this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next paragraph. "I was told that our soldiers knocked on the doors of the houses, and when the doors opened the soldiers sprayed the interior of the houses with gunfire eliminating everyone inside." Did you ever make this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the last paragraph on page 23 --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget the first sentence and we start from: "We began preparations for an attack on Bratunac. And then two days before the scheduled attack Naser Oric decided to attack Skelani instead." Do you remember having said this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we talked about that. I remember I said that there had been talks about whether to attack Bratunac or Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Skip the next three paragraphs and go to the paragraph which starts with: "Napad je izvrsen 16. Januara 1993." Do you find it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let me read -- the first two sentences or three sentences are not relevant to us. It's only the rest that I would like to ask you about. "The attack was launched 16 January, about 5.00 a.m. Certain units were tasked to do certain things. The main task was to capture Jezero. It was on top of a hill and a good position. Naser Oric assumed the hardest task of the offensive and that was to capture Kusica Groblje. It was a dominant, strong position. Zulfo Tursunovic and the others were supposed to cut off any logistical supply routes." Do you remember having said this, stating this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we discussed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are almost there. It's all coming to an end. Go to page 26, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to read anything except maybe one line from this paragraph. Could you please read it for yourself. In English it's page 25 and it starts first paragraph from the top it starts: "In the morning 'Zele' told me and I saw the chief of police." In B/C/S, page 26, first paragraph: "Ujutro mi je Zele to ispricao."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like you to read it for yourself, not aloud in other words, and then I will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In this paragraph you refer to another incident in which Kemo was supposedly involved. It's of no interest at all to this Trial Chamber; we don't want to hear about it. But towards the end of that paragraph you say: "After this Naser sent 'Kemo'", that is Kemal Mehmedovic, "to Tuzla." Do you remember stating this to the officer interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this. I remember when this happened. I didn't say he was sent by Naser. What I said was Kemo had left Srebrenica for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you never said that Naser sent Kemo to Tuzla; that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one could have sent Kemo anywhere. Kemo only belonged to himself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Skip the next paragraph, please, and we come to the paragraph which reads: "Ratno predsjednistvo nije nikakve vlasti."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And according to this statement what we have here is that you stated to the interviewing officer: "The War Presidency did not have any power over Naser Oric. They were all subjected to Naser Oric's control and power. These people were not necessarily Oric's men, but they were powerless to challenge Naser." Do you remember having stated this in your -- to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is out of context. I don't remember having this particular discussion. We talked about the competencies of the War Presidency and the army, and not about ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go to page 28, the penultimate paragraph, the one before the last. The English is page 27, four paragraphs from the bottom. Dr. Mujkanovic, did you find it? It starts with --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... "As far as I know when Naser spoke with Sefer Halilovic he was not using the code because I don't think he had Sarajevo codes." Did you ever state this to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we spoke about whether the line used when Naser spoke to Sefer was a coded line or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked you a few minutes ago to read that paragraph page 20 -- about Kemo, in other words.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 26, the first paragraph in your language.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that paragraph in the first sentence says: "In the morning Zele told me and I saw the chief of police." Did you make that statement? Did you tell the interviewing officer that after what Zele told you you saw the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why did you feel the need to see the chief of police, or was it just an accidental meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was accidental. Here it says that I went there, but Becir Bogilovic would very often come to the hospital. So it's not as if I went to see the chief of police; I saw him when he came to see me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I've been trying to follow as much with the utmost attention, I must say, your testimony, both when you were being examined in chief and during the cross-examination. I would like to have it clear in my mind for the benefit of the entire Trial Chamber what is your position in regard to who came or who was under Naser Oric's command when he was commander of the Srebrenica defence. Who was under his command?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the units that I have mentioned, which were in fact part of certain regions, villages, or groups of villages. And the units were composed of men from those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another matter of clarification that we need to come to. I take it, if I understood you well, that you were only physically present during one of the offensives and not more than one. The other instance you were further -- at quite a distance; you couldn't see what was happening. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was never present at any of the offensives; I was only present at an elevation with Ramzo Becirovic when Bjelovac was attacked. That was 3 or 4 kilometres from when the fighting was taking place and I was at Podravanje when the fighting had finished. Two days later I went to Hakija Meholjic's unit at Podravanje. That was when I was present there; it was immediately after the fighting. As for the other areas in which there was fighting, I was never present in those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's how I meant to put it. You also told us in the course of your testimony that a very small percentage of the fighters wore uniforms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when you were in Podravanje two days after the offensive and you noticed what you testified about, the plundering and the burning --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the persons that you saw doing these things, were they wearing civilian clothes or uniforms? You already told us that they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't armed. They were wearing civilian clothing. They weren't wearing uniforms. And when I say "uniforms," I mean camouflage uniforms which were worn by some of the combatants in Srebrenica. The clothes they were wearing were quite ordinary. They were wearing trousers of some kind, jackets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for all intents and purposes, would I be correct in taking it that those persons you saw plundering and setting buildings on fire could have actually been fighters as well, fighters not wearing uniforms --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure he said buildings. I thought in Podravanje it was a haystack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in Podravanje it was haystacks, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't this also speculation, pure and simple?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just asking him whether he would agree that because they were not wearing uniforms they could have been -- doesn't mean a thing. It could have been fighters as well and not just civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It could have been civilians or fighters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. In other words, would it be more -- would it be more correct to say that those were persons wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons were persons wearing civilian clothes. They didn't have any insignia on them, and in general no insignia was worn. No insignia were worn there. I have said that some of those in uniform had badges on their left arms. They had six golden lilies, an emblem consisting of six golden lilies. But there was nothing that indicated that they were combatants. But if we say that the civilians and combatants more or less wore the same sort of clothes, that's one way of looking at things. But on the whole these people were elderly people, women and children. I couldn't say that they were soldiers or combatants. It was a mob that would go there and gather everything that they got their hands on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please go to your second statement, the one from 2004, for a very -- two very short questions. And the very first page of that statement which should be page 2.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where you are referring to the document which was shown -- you were shown earlier on where members -- some members of the operation staff of Srebrenica tendered their resignation. And you are reported as having stated here --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "These persons did submit their resignations. All the reasons mentioned in this document for the reasons of resignation of the OS staff Srebrenica are genuine. Such conditions did exist at the time. OS staff Srebrenica was not given any importance by Naser Oric." Did you ever make that statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I gave this statement to the official and I was shown this document. I said that I had never seen the document before. But I said that I was aware of the fact that there were some people, the people mentioned there, who had resigned. And they continued to perform those duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next paragraph, paragraph 4, the second part of that paragraph which was also in part read out to you by Mr. Wubben earlier on. I'm going to read it to you again and once more I would ask you to kindly confirm to us whether you ever made this statement to the interviewing officer. "In fact, it was a kind of a public pressure to burn down the personal property left by the Serbs. Naser Oric was unable to stop that happening; he followed the public will. I think he should have been strict enough to stop the destruction of the property during the attacks; however, he chose the easy way out. He did not want to annoy the people and lose respect." Do you recall having ever made this statement to the interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser has some questions to you arising out of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to make it clear from the very outset, I will not refer to your prior statements, but only to your testimony which you gave in these days here at the court. But before coming to my questions, I would like to make a short comment with regard to the submission or the discussion which was made before the break with regard to taking resort to these prior statements, because one of the submissions was that this might perhaps not be in accordance with certain rules. And since the Presiding Judge comes from a common-law country with an adversarial system, I would like to make I say as a short comment as a Judge coming from a continental system: First of all, I think the Bench -- and I would like to address also to the public that there should not be the impression that the Bench is not paying due regard to the rules of the Statute and the Rules of Procedure -- this Court has to make a valid judgement and a judgement which has to be based on truth, and this is also expressed in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 90 (F)(i). Of course, finding the truth has to be done by fair means, but if there was the impression that fairness is only present in an adversarial system, I would not like to have kept this in the minds. Other criminal-procedure systems also do their best in preserving fairness, perhaps by different rules. If this Court is broadly, as was stated by the Defence, following the adversarial system, that does not mean that everything has to be as it is in an adversarial system. The term "adversarial" doesn't even appear in the procedure. And I would like to refer you to a very important provision in the rules of evidence which would say that Rule 89: "A Chamber shall apply the rules of evidence set forth in this section and shall not be bound by national rules of evidence." And if you go to Rule 85 where it speaks of the presentation of evidence it says some power given to the Bench, how to direct the presentation, in particular paragraph (B) would say that the Judges may put -- may put questions to the witness at any stage. Now, according to these rules I would like to ask the following questions, and again I do not refer to prior statements but only refer to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: First of all, may I come back, Dr. Mujkanovic, to your visits, the visit of Naser Oric in the hospital. You state that he came almost regularly. Now, did other commanders also come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Did they do the same thing as Naser Oric? What was -- what did they talk about?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They'd always come to ask about one of their combatants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Can you speak a little louder --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come to ask about the health of one of their combatants. Other commanders would come to ask about the health of their combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, in one of your statements it was on page 50 -- 5120, you stated as testified When Naser Oric came, we usually discussed the weapons that had been seized. Now, did this having to do with the health of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't have anything to do with the health of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And what does it mean, the seized weapons? Seized by whom?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, Your Honour Mr. Eser, Naser would come after the actions. He was interested in the health of the soldiers -- the combatants and afterwards they would always have time to speak about the matter. And most frequently he would speak about the weapons that had been seized because that was of greatest importance to him, the weapons that had been seized in the course of the action carried out by the Srebrenica combatants in the villages that we have referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now another statement was that local commanders saw Naser Oric as their commander of said area in Srebrenica. Now, what local commanders are you referring to in this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to all the commanders. I could list them. I could provide you with their first and last names, but I'm referring to all the commanders who are in command of the units that we have been speaking about throughout my testimony, with the exception of one Hakija Mehuric. This included Zulfo Tursunovic, Akif Ustic, Ahmo Tihic, Senahid Tabakovic. It's difficult for me to remember all the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: All these commanders would see Naser Oric as their commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked a similar question about Zulfo and it was disallowed. I asked if Zulfo would consider that Naser to have authority about him and I was not allowed to put that questions because it was considered to be speculation. This witness doesn't know what Zulfo thought about Naser or whether he considered to be under his command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I was phrasing verbatim, local commanders -- as testified by the witness, local commanders saw Naser as their commander of said area in Srebrenica. I was only asking to whom commanders he was referring to. So...

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to looting and burning, we have already touched this problem and you reiterated just to Judge -- to the Presiding Judge that it was difficult to distinguish with regard to uniforms whether civilians had has uniforms or soldiers had no uniforms. So how was it possible to distinguish at all whether looting, taking things away, or even burning was committed by the one and not by the others? Do you have any indications how you may distinguish? You made this distinction.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the discussion we had on the problem of attempting to prevent looting and burning, even if it is -- might have been impossible to -- just one last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can it take this question? No. We have to stop because they have to change the tape. We'll stay here and finish with the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say I certainly have a number of questions for this witness arising from Your Honours' questions and new areas which have been raised by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we might as well have a break straightaway. We'll have a break of 20, 25 minutes, which would leave us with -- we need to also discuss and decide upon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to discuss very shortly and decide on your motion for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I have I would say half an hour with this witness. I would prefer to deal, if necessary, with the adjournment application tomorrow if we run out of time today. It's less important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. What is important is to finish with this witness and send him back home. Yes, Dr. Wubben [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In addition to the issue of the motion, we could be short in that respect. It's also of importance to update the Victims and Witnesses Unit in regard to the witness who is now present and that should be organised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. This witness will finish today. I have not put any restrictions on any of you. He has to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What I mean is a request to deal with that motion right after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll start at 6.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I? I just have heard what Mr. Wubben is saying about dealing with that motion. This is a very important witness. He's been testifying for days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You'll have all the time to finish your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we start at 6.00, you've got half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to be as short as possible. And I have a question with regard to the taking away property, but in particular food. And on the last days you testified that the only thing that the troops took were weapons and ammunitions. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, on other occasions you would say the following -- that was 5275 -- it's on page 57 -- 5275 to give you an idea of what I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, could we have the day, please, so I can find it on our LiveNote transcript. Otherwise I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just a minute. 5275. That was on the -- on Thursday, 17th. You have been asked with regard to: Do you understand that a lot of food and a lot of medicine were also captured at Fakovici? And your answer was: "A certain amount of medicines and medical supplies were brought in fact, but I cannot speak about the quantities of food that were captured." So I would -- can we conclude from this statement that not only medicine but also certain quantities of food have been captured, and if so by whom?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that all these actions were started because of food. It's the same as I've already explained. The civilians who were waiting would storm the villages in order to get food and later also other items that they would then trade for food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And on another occasion that was on Tuesday, on page 5128 you testified: "The main reason why the action was organised" - that was Voljavica, Zaluzje, Bjelovac - "the main reason why the action was organised -- why the attack was organised was to get hold of food, materiel, technical supplies, medicines, and everything else that was required for the normal functioning of the free territory of Srebrenica." So can we conclude from this that not only weapons have been taken away but also food or other items?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Mr. Eser, what I have said is that after a certain village was taken people would grab whatever they believed they needed. In addition to food, they would take technical appliances, refrigerators. CB sets, electrical ovens. I don't see how they could use these things as there was no electricity in Srebrenica. They believed these were items that could come in useful for trading, in exchange for food. So whatever they thought they might be able to put to some use, they took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But since you have testified that it was very difficult to distinguish between soldier fighters and civilians, because fighters may have had uniforms or not, and the similar way civilians may have had uniforms or not. Now, how can you -- how is it possible to say whether these items which you mentioned have only been taken away by civilians and not perhaps also by fighters?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already, and I repeat now: Most of the population, most of the people referred to as hapci or hapci units, as mentioned in the book, those groups were made up mostly of women and children. There was snow on the ground, so they would put things on ovens, put ropes on the oven and drag these off. But those of these individuals were women, elderly persons, and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So my last question with regard to the storage as Potocari we had talked about -- I am now referring to Wednesday, page 5155 where you testified: "I learned in Naser Oric's house where he lived there was a storage and that is where some of the ammunition was kept. So this was in his house. There was also some food storage there, and this was also for the purposes of the army." Now my question is: Where did this food come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: To your knowledge. To your knowledge. To your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say where the food came from. But I assume it was from the villages that had been taken. Those were no large quantities of food, rather minute quantities that Naser used to distribute to his better fighters, to those who were particularly brave, to help their families to survive. As I said, what the fighters cared about the most was to get hold of food and ammunition. These civilians who would storm the villages later hardly had time to do anything else but grab food and take it back to their families. But the same applied to the fighters because they also lived in homes with their families. So that was one of the reasons. And the storage facility that there was inside his house -- first of all it's a very small house. You couldn't hold large quantities of food or ammunition there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Does this mean that since the fighters were living in their families, when they had been in the village that they would also take, beside ammunition, also food home, perhaps they may have even been expected to take food home?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I asked questions of this nature, it was objected date unspecific, time unspecific, speculative. I think that question is all those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Sir, I am referring to attacks that are part of the indictment. Let's take Fakovici or Bjelovac. When soldiers living -- or fighters living in their families, would they only take away or clear the village, or would they also take certain things, for instance food, back to their own families?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to answer that question. In fact, I don't think I can. I would merely be speculating as to what actually was the case. The fact is fighters lived with their families. Whether their women were the first to get there and snatch the food is something that I can't say. I am not a witness who can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in the realm of speculation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. So Mr. Jones, I understand has got some questions. Please try to finish, Mr. Jones, and allow some time for the discussion, brief discussion on your motion because I can tell you more or less because we have already discussed it amongst ourselves what the position is but we have to make things clear to the organisation of the Tribunal obviously. Plus we need some information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And for my part it's more important to deal with this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. We owe it to the witness to send him home today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for the technical difficulties. I think I'm okay now. Further cross-examination by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, just a few final questions arising from the questions which have been put from the Bench, firstly concerning the relationship between Naser Oric and Zulfo Tursunovic. You told us last week that Zulfo was an independent character. You described him a little. Today in answer to His Honour's question, you mentioned him as one of the commanders being under Oric. My question is I want you to consider the real situation, the actual reality of the relationship between the two men. Considering their personalities, did you -- do you think or did you see Naser Oric ordering Zulfo Tursunovic around? Was that possible?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Naser order Zulfo Tursunovic around. Zulfo was also a person of highly disputable character. He takes nothing from anyone. He's a very exclusive person, and I said so when I talked about Zulfo Tursunovic. He would occasionally come down to Srebrenica. It would happen once a week or once a fortnight. Whenever he came, everyone gave him a wide berth. No one wanted to be near him because he was a violent man. He would sometimes use firearms, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are repeating now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and if you could give brief answers, if possible. Do you exclude the possibility that Zulfo acted independently, as an independent commander of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand the question. Do I exclude the possibility -- I'm not sure I got the latter part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me do it this way: Is it possible that Zulfo Tursunovic in fact acted as an independent commander, at least in certain matters or certain actions?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most of the cases he ran an entire area and he wouldn't let anyone interfere with his job. If there was something he liked, he would accept it, but he was a very exclusive person. He ran the Susica area and he wouldn't allow anyone near. You couldn't even go there unless you had been invited there by him specifically; that was the only way you could go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that include Naser Oric, that he could only go in that area if invited?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applied to everyone, Naser and everyone else, including myself. I was never allowed to go. I did go to see him twice, but both times I was picked up by him in person. That was the only way you could get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked also about Motorolas. Isn't that right that you don't know how they were used or if they were used at all in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how Motorolas are used because I never used one myself. I saw that Hakija Meholjic had one or two sets of these. He had one and Velid Delic had the other. I know they had those Motorolas. Hakim was a police officer and it was probably an item inherited from the MUP, the former MUP, for communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown a passage in your 2000 statement where you talked about Naser Oric's command encompassing 12.000 people. Now I want to preface my question by the following: You told us about siege in the enclave, shelling lack of uniforms, lack of rules, the absence of barracks, the absence of an armoury, the fact that salaries weren't paid. Now, given that, are you saying that Naser Oric had effective real control over 12.000 fighters in Srebrenica, or are you saying something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think in the part that I read to him from the statement it said 12.000 was the number, but the ones who were fighters, soldiers as it is in the statement, amounted to 10.000, not 12.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even for 10.000 people, are you saying that Naser Oric had control over each and every one of those 10.000 people?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've said this. He has no control whatsoever over Hakim Meholjic's unit. He may have had partial control over Zulfo Tursunovic's unit, and I have already explained what their relationship was like. He has no control over Akif Ustic's unit. I can't say exactly what their respective strengths were of these units. I mean -- but if we consider these to be formal units, those were units beyond his control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that when you refer to that -- those 10.000 people, you're actually saying that there were 10.000 able-bodied men in the enclave of 80.000 people?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all what I would like to tell the Trial Chamber is that the figure used and cited here is something that was never officially endorsed. I never received a document based on which I could judge that there were 10.000 or 12.000 combatants. This was a speculative figure. The same applies to the actual numbers of people living in the area, the local population. Those were just guesswork, the figures. I wouldn't stick to these therefore, this figure, about the 10.000 or 12.000 people who defended Srebrenica. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So the 10.000 -- that figure refers to the people who were defending Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us last week that the War Presidency was the supreme authority in Srebrenica. Today you were asked about whether Fejzic was under Naser Oric, so to speak. It's right, isn't it, that Hamdija Fejzic was not the President of the War Presidency, firstly, was he?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Hamdija Fejzic was President of the Executive Board of this sort of War Presidency, and the President of the War Presidency was Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right, sir, that you don't know the power relationship, if I can describe it that way, between Fejzic and Oric or between Avdic and Oric when you were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. The power relationship -- I'm not sure I understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not able to say, are you, whether Fejzic deferred to Naser Oric or whether Avdic deferred to Naser Oric or vice versa, are you? That's something beyond your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, is it right also - and we saw this in your statement - where it appears that you said Naser Oric saw you as competition. Is it right that that's not something which you ever said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's told us that already I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no you're perfectly entitled to ask him the question. I took him when he answered my question that he did not confirm that he ever stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, taking that answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But please do put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you never said that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. I don't think you could compare Naser's role to my role. I was a surgeon. I'm not sure how I could have aspired to anything in particular or pose a threat of competition to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
