utterances.text: Do you feel that generally looking at the passages of the statement, 2000 statement, which you've been shown that it distorts what you told the investigators?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was shown the Bosnian version of the statement, I said that it was not consistent with the spirit of my interview. I said it right at the outset. I said there were entire portions that were simply not consistent or were taken out of the overall context of my account, and even worded in the first person as if I had been saying: I did so-and-so and not presented in a more global light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But once we are on this matter. I put it to you that this particular reference that you were asked to comment about and which I asked you before, in other words the part where according to the statement you say that after your insistence to have in place an operations headquarters, Oric was against it and considered you as a competition, you're telling us that you never said that. But when you were proofed before you started your evidence by the Prosecution, you did not say anything about this particular part of the statement. Is that correct? You were proofed -- when you arrived here in The Hague you were shown your statement in the Serbian language --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there were several corrections that you made to it, several points that you made in relation to that statement saying that it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is not one of them. I put it to you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not something that we discussed. Whenever we came to a session that I discussed with Mr. Wubben, I would always say so and specify the corrections I wanted made, but there were plenty of things there that we never even got down to discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And following on from that, it's not true to say, is it, that proofing notes reflect all of your disagreement with the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the point I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if that's clear. Hopefully that's a matter between the parties which should be abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not the witness can answer this question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, he is saying that what you have here is the result of what you discussed, but it is not excluding that there are other points in the witness -- in the statement that he doesn't agree with and that he didn't comment about because he was not asked about those particular parts. This is what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a matter we can discuss in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not important because as I said, we are only looking at the statements from a relative point of view and not as testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you can see my concern is I don't want it to be thought that the only corrections in the proofing notes are the only differences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the point I wanted to make. And that's why I intervened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Mujkanovic, when you told the investigators that you weren't happy with the statement as a summary, what you said, how did they react?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it first thing in the morning at our meeting. I said there were a lot of things there that were out of context. I showed them entire portions of the document, and I was told not to pay that much attention to what the statement said, that the Trial Chamber would only take into account my personal testimony. I was told that everything that was hearsay, everything that I could not substantiate in terms of who I heard it from was not something I should work with, was not something that I should base any conclusions on. I was told that the judicial system in my country attaches more importance to oral statements. But for this Trial Chamber, the most important thing would be whatever I say during my testimony, and that only this would be evaluated. There were quite a number of things that we didn't even touch upon. We did make some corrections whenever we came across things that needed correcting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I've got still about 20 questions. I'll be grateful if we could -- if you could answer with a yes or no where possible, because I only have about 15 minutes. Firstly, concerning authorisation to use the radio and you being told that Naser Oric had to grant such authorisation. Is it right that you were only told that once?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean only told that once?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that something which was told to you on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once. Becirevic, who operated the radio equipment, was the one who told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you also told us that Naser Oric informed you that he was reporting to Sefer Halilovic. Isn't it right that you don't know for a fact whether or not Oric did report to Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, Naser Oric never spoke to me about whom he reported to. I heard about this from Becirevic, Ibrahim. When I was in the post office, he would say for example Well, I have provided a connection with Sarajevo, et cetera, so I was never present when Naser Oric spoke to, let's say, Sefer Halilovic. So there's nothing I could say about that. I couldn't say that this is something I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. You were also asked today about a passage in your 2000 statement where it was said that: There wasn't much of an interest in capturing Serb soldiers." But you also refer -- it's page 23 of your statement: "At Skelani a passage was made so that Serbs could get away." Now, is it right to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did not read that paragraph to him. And in any case, it's not important because we don't have in the charges killing during offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It was just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Killings in the prison in Srebrenica. So it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just that statement refers to passage being made so soldiers can escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You might as well forget it because it's of no importance or consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about a statement in your 2000 statement where you talked about three waves of people coming into villages. Isn't it right that you never actually saw three waves of people come in one after the other in the way that was set out in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally I didn't see that. I was speaking about Podravanje, about when I saw some people who were there and -- well, I've testified about this. I won't go into it again. But there was a rumour in Srebrenica according to which there were three waves. The first wave consisted of people who would take out what was essential; and then there was a second wave would go there in search of other items; and then a third wave consisting of people who would go and search for items with sticks of some kind to probe the ground, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a rumour which you heard?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you also were asked possibly to speculate about whether houses were burnt down possibly to prevent Serbs from returning, and you accepted that possibility. So following on from that, your acceptance of that possibility, I put it to you that it's also possible that houses were burnt so that Serbs wouldn't come back and shell and snipe and shoot from those houses. Do you accept that possibility?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also possible. I've expressed my personal opinion. There will probably be other witnesses who will be in a better position to clarify this for you; that's also a possibility though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We also saw in your 2000 statement reference to Naser as a king with huge powers. But here you've told about us as him as a 25 years old with rivalries with other commanders. And when I put it to you that he was drunk with power, you said what power. So is it right that you do not maintain that Naser was a king with absolute powers in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I asked him the question, he told us that he does not confirm that he ever said that to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I can withdraw that question if that's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, page 19 at the top of your -- page 19 of the 2000 statement at the top it's stated: "Oric was the person in charge of maintaining a professionally organised operation." You don't need to look at it, you can take that phrase "professionally organised operation." Now, isn't that right that there wasn't such thing as a professionally organised operation the whole time you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I've been speaking about the fact that Srebrenica didn't have an organised army for six days now. They didn't have combatants; the civilian authorities hadn't been authorised; the judicial authorities didn't exist. Everything had been improvised. So when I speak of my job as a doctor, as a surgeon, when I speak about the fact that that was improvisation, everything was improvised. So it's for you to draw your own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I won't ask you about the actions because I think it's clear. You stated that you don't know who -- that Naser Oric was present at any of those actions. Skelani was briefly touched on. Are you aware that in fact the Skelani people, if I can put it that way, Ahmo Tihic and others, outvoted Naser Oric who was in favour of attacking Bratunac, contrary to what is set out in your 2000 statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were two options, two possibilities, either Bratunac or Skelani. As to how the decision was taken, as to how they decided which direction they should go to, I couldn't say. But I know that there were events that took place in Skelani. I don't know how this happened, but I also know that the opinion prevailed according to which Skelani was part of Srebrenica municipality. And that by taking Skelani, the entire municipality of Srebrenica would in a sense be liberated; whereas an attack on Bratunac would have resulted in the fact that Srebrenica would still be under Serbian occupation. That's what I heard, but I wasn't present at any meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you're going at a tangent around and around and around and you're not answering the question. The question very simply put to you was the following: You said or you are reported in your statement - and you confirmed to me when I put the statement to you - that all -- after that the operations staff had been planning to attack Bratunac, Oric two days before decided to attack Skelani instead. It's been put to you by Mr. Jones that even if Oric decided two days before to attack Skelani instead, it's not because he wanted to attack Skelani but because he had been overruled by Avdic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, by Ahmo Tihic and was outvoted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Outvoted by Ahmo Tihic and others. Are you aware of this or not? And answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, next question. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us how the War Presidency operated on the basis of one man, one vote, and you said it was the ultimate authority. It may be an obvious point, but it's right, then, it's not true to say, is it, that Oric controlled the War Presidency, that he had it in the palm of his hand; that's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. The War Presidency, that's not something that I said. Never once did I say that Naser Oric controlled the War Presidency. I said that the War Presidency was the highest organ of power in Srebrenica. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We also saw in the 2004 statement discussion, again, of the resignations of the operations staff. And we saw a document with your testimony in which Osman Osmanovic was proposing an appointment to the War Presidency. In your 2004 statement it says that Naser Oric didn't give much importance to the operations staff. Now, I put it to you that that's because he was no part of that structure, of the operations staff structure. Do you accept that that might be why it was not important to him that his formation --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't in the operations staff; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at this question again of doing the impossible, preventing civilians from burning villages, you've explained how villages were miles apart on hilly terrain. We've seen this expression of Oric taking the easy way out. There is no non-easy way out, was there? There was nothing that could be done.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and this is something we have been discussing all along, and I still claim that no one could have done anything in that situation, neither Naser Oric or someone with even more authority. Even the established organs of power couldn't have done anything. I tried to clarify the situation to the Chamber, I tried to explain the structure of the villages. There may be one house on one hill, another on another hill, and a distance of many kilometres between these two hills. It was impossible to control such a vast area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just to be complete, Your Honour, the question was Was there nothing that could be done of course, as far as the witness is aware?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. We could get another witness come forward and say that everything could be done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just three final questions. You were asked about civilians and how given the lack of uniforms it was difficult to tell whether someone was a civilian or a fighter. But isn't that right that you also told us that women, children and old people looted? And would you accept that those people are not fighters? Let me leave it that way.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you about what I saw in Podravanje. There were women, children, elderly people. That was the group of people -- not a group of people. There were a thousand people there; that's certain. At various locations. And they were taking items out of the warehouses over there, and I said that I saw them set fire to an excavator that was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to women, children, elderly people, you refer to them as civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. No women participated in the defence of Srebrenica. I didn't see a single woman who was a combatant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two final questions. One concerns this storage facility in Potocari that you've been asked about today. Isn't that right that that was the house where Naser Oric's mother and father lived, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the house I referred to. Oric's father and mother lived there, his brother, and Oric himself, Naser Oric himself. I'm referring to the same house, not to some other house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see food stored there yourself? Did you go there and see the food stored?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept that there were other sources of food besides what was looted, in other words food from convoys, from home-made bread, from air drops?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I told the Trial Chamber. The first convoy entered towards the end of November 1992, the second one seven days later. And then there was a certain period of time until March 1993 when there were no convoys, until mid-March. There were certain sources of food, but they weren't sufficient for the entire population there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one final question. Quite apart from the impossibility of stopping civilians from looting food, do you agree that from what you saw of the public-health situation that if those people were prevented from taking food, many of them would have starved to death?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were cases of starvation. It's been recorded by journalists who were there. There were people who starved to death as a result of not eating anything for 10, 12, or 13 days. And they were also malnourished. A quarter of the food wasn't sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you don't have any further questions, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the opportunity and thank you, Witness, for your full answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have procedural right for that, to that opportunity. So I thank you, Mr. Jones, for having cooperated and finished in good time. Dr. Mujkanovic, we have come to the end. We did our best to make sure to finish with your testimony today so you are free to go now. You will be escorted by our usher. On behalf of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take it you presume that I have no questions. But I want to confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I do by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so because you had an opportunity to indicate that before and you didn't, so I assume that you didn't. So you will be escorted by our usher very soon. And on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and on my own behalf I would like to thank you for coming over. It hasn't been easy for you because it's a long time that you have been here and I appreciate your cooperation with this Tribunal. My last words to you before you leave this courtroom is that on behalf of everyone present here we wish you a safe journey back home and thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's do this quickly. I do not intend to stay one second more than 7.00 because I think we've had too much cooperation from everyone. So I don't want to -- anyone. You have a motion, you would like this Trial Chamber not to proceed from now on, having finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can modify the motion to this extent: Today I was in touch with -- are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session because this is one of the things because of course I am going to ask you what the situation is because, apart from the motion itself, we need to plan. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Following the debate we have just had, the position of the Tribunal is as follows: It appears that Madam Vidovic is indisposed and that she requires some time, a short time, relatively speaking, before she can recommence her role as lead counsel and attend the sittings. The Trial Chamber has also heard the Prosecution, that does not -- after having heard Mr. Jones does not object to an adjournment until Madam Vidovic returns and is in the position to resume the -- her role and cross-examine the next two witnesses. Consequently, there will be a rescheduling and there will be an interval of time in which we will not sit. And this is expected to be of a short duration because Madam Vidovic is expected to return to work sometime next week and then should be in a position to take over again shortly after that. The position of the Tribunal is that if there is any substantial change in the circumstances or if there is even the slight indication that Madam Vidovic's return could be delayed further than has been indicated by you, Mr. Jones, then I need the commitment -- your commitment that you will communicate this to the registrar straightaway, in other words that you will communicate with us straightaway and also with the Prosecution so that we will decide what's best needed in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I can certainly undertake to give the most detailed and regular updates to both your staff and the Prosecution to keep you abreast of the latest developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The other thing is that I would appreciate if you could file privately and in confidential -- confidentially a -- an indication of what the problem is so that on -- from our part we can also make our own assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate your cooperation. The other thing is this: We have a meeting scheduled for Friday to discuss you-know-what. Do I cancel that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I can attend on behalf of our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the meeting we have at Friday at 2.30 stays, remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last -- so the meeting stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last thing is: This has been a difficult sitting more or less, and I needed the cooperation of everyone. In particular, I want to thank the staff, technical, interpreters, the rest, you, Mr. Jones; the registry for having been kind enough to supply us with an interpreter without which we couldn't have proceeded today; and I thank you you, Madam, for your cooperation. We'll meet again on Friday in my room. Thank you.
